title: Scripture's authority is received immediately — not proved from Scripture
source_text: XVIII. Habere quidem debent prima fidei principia divinitatis & veritatis suae notas & characteres, & argumenta quibus probentur & suadeantur: sed directe & proprie seipsa probare non possunt: nec etiam ab aliis pendent fidei principiis, unde authoritatem & fidem mutuentur. Jam vero prima illa religionis regula, & Christianae fidei principia nobis sunt Scripturae divinae constantes certo numero librorum θεοπνεύστων. Ac proinde sacrae Scripturae authoritas, juxta sententiam nostram, ex ipsa Scriptura probari non debet, sed ab omnibus Christianis immediate & propter se suscipi.
pass_a_gloss: Indeed the first principles of faith ought to have marks and characters of their divinity and truth, and arguments by which they are proved and urged: but directly and properly they cannot prove themselves; nor do they depend on other principles of faith from which they would borrow authority and credit. Now that first rule of religion, and the principles of Christian faith, are for us the divine Scriptures consisting in a fixed number of God-breathed books. And therefore the authority of sacred Scripture, according to our judgment, ought not to be proved from Scripture itself, but to be received by all Christians immediately and for its own sake.
pass_b_english: Faith's first principles must bear marks and characters of their divinity and truth, and arguments that recommend them. But they cannot, directly and properly, prove themselves. Nor do they lean on other faith principles from which they would borrow authority.
That first rule of religion — the principles of Christian faith — is for us the divine Scriptures, a fixed set of God-breathed books (θεοπνεύστων).
So on our view Scripture's authority should not be proved from Scripture itself. All Christians receive it immediately, and for its own sake.

choices.why: Keeps Pauline Greek; OCR garbled swerd/swr.

rejected: because of itself alone as circular proof
